doc.title: Ruthie Foster interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 28, 2023

title: Austin City Limits and keeping instrumentation sparse
summary: Rowe recalls her sparse Austin City Limits set; she says she keeps the song up front as a songwriter first.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: It was a number of years ago when I saw you on Austin City Limits, not the most recent time but it was a small group. You had a woman who provided vocal harmonies and some percussion. And I was hooked from the get-go. It was late at night, I got home from a gig and I was just sort of winding down. And again, serendipity, I landed on this. And if I can recall the feeling it just seemed that even though the instrumentation was sparse that’s all that was required at that time.

Yeah. I think that has a lot to do with — keeping the instrumentation sparse was important for me. It had a lot to do with my wanting to keep the song up front. It’s about the song for me, and I am a songwriter. I like to call myself a singer, but I love to think that I’m a songwriter first and that’s important for instrumentation on stage. And yeah, I remember that night. I had a guitar player, drummer, bass player, and I think Cyd, Cyd Cassone was on percussion that night. Yeah, we kept it pretty simple. Pretty much the way my stage show was during that period.
